pull.title: net: stop monitoring select exceptions outside Windows
pull.body:
Alternative approach to #36688, citing the relevant parts of its description:

> There is currently nothing preventing us to receive TCP urgent data, which would never be returned by `recv()`. Linux's `poll()` is indifferent to this, but the `select()` socket monitoring may keep reporting it as pending on some platforms.
> 
> This would not prevent progress nor lead to a crash anymore after #36665, but it's still undesirable.

Fix this by ignoring the exceptionSet. Except on Windows, where we instead disconnect if its used.

We could instead have set `SO_OOBINLINE` on our sockets, so `recv()` returns any urgent data sent to us (and likely leads us to disconnect the peer). RFC 6093 doesn't forbid this, but the current approach seems more clear and direct to me.

The PR makes two additional changes for clarity:
- wrap the `FD_ISSET` check in `#ifdef WIN32` (no behavior change)
- instead of `if (recvSet || errorSet)`, check `errorSet` separately and earlier (emits a different log message)

Test coverage is introduced in `p2p_socket_errors.py`.

Finally a similar fix is applied to HTTP.

sock: guard select exception result handling with WIN32

The select() backend only adds sockets to the exception set on Windows.
Elsewhere, the set starts empty and remains empty after select(), so
checking it with FD_ISSET() is a no-op. Match the existing WIN32 guard
around FD_SET().

This commit does not change behavior.

events.body:
I dropped the comment-only commit.

Added two commits based on @vasild's feedback.

Also added and expanded @pinheadmz's tests.

Finally, I added the http fix at the end. It should be simple to review since it's the same approach.

I also tested on Windows native.

> We could instead have set `SO_OOBINLINE` on our sockets, so `recv()` returns any urgent data sent to us (and likely leads us to disconnect the peer). RFC 6093 doesn't forbid this, but the current approach seems more clear and direct to me.

I believe it's possible to construct an oob urgent ptr for data which will never be sent and which will then never be received but will still trigger the exception set. Setting SO_OOBINLINE thus can't ultimately clear the select() exception because no data is actually inline to read. On the BSDs I examined (and therefore likely OS/X) this will still generate an exception so the current select() call will return immediately again. As noted elsewhere, this doesn't technically prevent eventual node progress.

fwiw, I strongly suggest that oob data be considered an error condition based on this. There is nowhere for UNIX-y OSes which an oob byte will ever be generated by a valid p2p peer, and thus it'll only ever be generated in this context — therefore disconnection is a logical and completely fair result. I personally think at this point it's worth a ban.

(Uh, just to be clear, at the very least I think we should delete the exceptfds from the select() call entirely, so strong ACK for this approach.)

> I strongly suggest that oob data be considered an error condition based on this

I agree that if there was a `DISCONNECT_ON_OOB` flag, we should set it. But we can't directly detect if such data was present. All we can know is that `errorSet` was triggered, which could be for unrelated OS reasons. That could cause us to disconnect a well behaved peer.

That's why this PR simply ignores the exception set (outside Windows), instead of trying to handle it. It might be possible with poll(), but that would be better for a followup.

@midnightmagic agreed.

Imo we should just always disconnect when an exception is set, or when oob/prio are found. I don't see any need for platform-specific behavior here. I'd rather go with: https://github.com/theuni/bitcoin/commits/net-oob-error/

That branch unifies the select/poll behaviors, and causes a disconnect (on all platforms) if any of those conditions are true.

It differs from what's here in that it turns `POLLHUP` into a read event as it should be, rather than an error. That simplifies things significantly, as it allows draining to happen naturally, and it means that the exception set is truly only comprised of exceptions.

If receiving is off (meaning that we have data to send) and we receive a SIGHUP, we'll disconnect on the next send.

It fixes up the tests to show that OOB data always causes a disconnect.

comments.body:
This does not follow, and regardless that seems like a confusing comment to add here.

My reading of RFC 6093 is that it 1) discourages applications from sending urgent data 2) advises applications to set SO_OOBINLINE to fix the broken out of band mechanism regardless of their use for urgent data.

But regardless, i think that comment just adds more confusion than it clears up, and it would be better to drop it.

comments.body:
> 1) discourages applications from sending urgent data

The RFC says:

> Even though applications SHOULD NOT employ the urgent mechanism

This isn't about a misbehaving sender, but rather about application design (both sides).

> This does not follow

I'm not sure what exactly "this" refers to. It's true that the RFC does not forbid applications from setting `SO_OOBINLINE` if they don't "employ urgent indications".

I do think it's good to document that we don't "employ urgent indications". The absence of the setting implies it, but an actual code comment is more clear.

In any case, I'll drop the comment commit.

> Should the below `if (recvSet || errorSet)` be revised as well?

I added a commit to check `errorSet` separately and earlier, for `poll()`.

I spent some time trying to understand if that's a behavior change, but AFAIK it just emits a different log message. I added a test to demonstrate that.
